newsitem.title: UK: Unilever profits rise on East Asia, Europe.
newsitem.headline: Unilever profits rise on East Asia, Europe.

text.p: Anglo-Dutch foods and consumer products group Unilever NV/plc said Friday first-quarter profits rose to 538 million pounds ($873.2 million), driven by stronger sales in the Far East and higher profit margins on perfume in Europe.
"If I had to highlight two particular factors it would be the margin improvement in Europe and the big increase at operating level from Southeast Asia," said Unilever press officer Mike Haines.
The company posted a surprisingly strong 16 percent rise in its first-quarter trading profits to 661 million pounds ($1.1 billion), before one-time items.

The charges rose to 76 million pounds ($123.4 million) from 15 million ($24.4 million) a year ago, mainly due to changes at its foods businesses in Europe including a charge for a head office closure in Bristol.

Europe was Unilever's star performer with profits up 106 million pounds ($172.1 million) to 360 million ($584.4 million). Although sales rose just 1 percent, margins improved 2.6 percent to 9.4 percent.
Margins were lifted by a pensions benefit and the absence of a write-off in the 1996 first quarter of 14 million pounds ($22.7 million) due to the beef crisis.

Europe gained especially from higher sales of personal products, led by deodorants like Lynx in Britain, perfumes after the launch of cKbe in several countries and the rollout of Elizabeth Arden Fifth Avenue outside Britain, said Haines.
The exceptionally warm weather over Easter boosted ice cream and deodorant sales, he said.

Unilever's Asia-Pacific business showed a 17 million pound ($27.6 million) increase in trading profit to 107 million ($173.7 million) with a strong performance from Thailand and the Philippines on sales of Unilever's home and personal care products, said Haines.
Sales of detergents Viso and Haso in Vietnam grew, while India put in a very strong performance. After a difficult period Australia showed good sales growth in personal care products, he added.

But profits in North America fell by 11 percent as foods and prestige businesses made a slow start to the year after a strong end to 1996. In Latin America, trading profits were affected by increased marketing investment and higher costs in Brazil.
The contribution to group profits from Africa and the Middle East almost halved to 17 million pounds ($27.6 million) as sales fell after a major shake-up of distribution in Turkey.
